data.title: Anthropic's record IPO raises hopes for a charitable windfall that has nonprofits preparing to scale
data.description:
NEW YORK — It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco company's chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organised by an academic fellowship. As Kaplan recalls, he and Amodei spent the ride discussing "this idea of thoroughly investigating what kinds of charitable causes could do the most good".

"We had so much largesse to, sort of, disperse," Kaplan joked at a Hertz Foundation discussion in April 2025.

Those once-hypothetical philanthropic ambitions gained new steam as Anthropic debuted on the stock market to a record US$1.5 trillion (S$1.9 trillion) valuation. 

The Claude AI tool maker already plans to dedicate five per cent of its shares for a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its seven co-founders say they'll give away 80 per cent of their equity — a US$112 billion commitment based on its IPO price.

Now suddenly affluent employees, many of whom will become millionaires as they sell their vested stock, may wield enough capital to make transformative donations themselves - riches that are commanding the attention of nonprofits looking to direct some sliver toward causes from global health to animal welfare.

Silicon Valley has great expectations. The napkin math suggests leading US AI firms' valuations could add at least US$37 billion annually in intended philanthropy, according to a widely circulated May blog post by Nan Ransohoff, head of public goods at the payments company Stripe.

"This is a once-in-a-lifetime kind of opportunity for people to really make an impact on extreme poverty," said Peter Singer, the moral philosopher whose writings influence many tech donors.

Nonprofits aren't counting on an immediate charitable windfall, though. Many Anthropic employees cannot sell or gift the bulk of their shares until next spring. 

Questions persist about the charitable priorities of these potential philanthropists whose worldviews have been shaped by the increasingly powerful AI models advancing at breakneck speed. 

The sector's volatility — between high borrowing costs, recent turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia and warnings about risks to humanity — leaves skeptics doubtful about the amounts actually available to redistribute.

"The challenge is that deploying philanthropic capital is hard," said Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg, whose nonprofit matches funders with scientific initiatives. "That's not an automatic step."

AI philanthropists are expected to make large donations quickly

Will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?

There's reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute's Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have "actually managed to empty the safe" is low.

The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism. Titans such as oil magnate John D. Rockefeller Sr. and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie established bureaucratic institutions intended to address the root causes of social problems. 

Those were followed by the turn-of-the-century technology wealth that brought a more data-centric, risk-taking approach. The Gates Foundation launched to address pressing crises in global health and poverty.

AI wealth, according to Soskis, carries a sense of "extreme peril" and "really transformative promise" that should spur even more urgent action from this emerging class of donors.

At least one of Anthropic's co-founders will donate in the coming weeks to the Trump Accounts children's savings programme, according to comments made Friday by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC.

Anthropic's explosive growth is also fueling some anticipation that its 5,300 employees will want to rapidly scale their charitable impact, too. A generous internal giving programme adds another incentive. 

Employee equity gifts are matched by the company with shares of Class N common stock. Anthropic also partners with donor-advised fund vendors such as Daffy, which offer a tax-efficient tool for grantmaking without the hassle of a more sophisticated charitable foundation.

Daffy CEO Adam Nash expects this younger generation to give more quickly.

"The people working in AI see the impact AI is having already," Nash said. "And they are giving now, right?"

Tech-adjacent nonprofits prepare for influx

One organisation in particular appears poised to move those rising donation volumes.

Coefficient Giving was formed by San Francisco-based billionaire Cari Tuna and her husband, Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder and early Anthropic investor. A spokesperson told The New York Times the couple transferred their Anthropic stake into an undisclosed nonprofit last year to avoid personally profiting.

The philanthropic funder — which has directed more than US$8 billion since 2014 in support of global health, animal rights, AI safety and the effective altruism community — has been scaling its pledges. In July, Coefficient Giving increased its commitment to the grantmaker GiveWell to US$1 billion.

The move reflected expectations of "considerably more future funding for this kind of work," according to the announcement.

"We might grow a lot, in part because we want to spend faster in response to these trends," Coefficient Giving CEO Alexander Berger said during a late July public discussion. 

"But there is a great deal of room for other organisations and approaches, and I do not expect us to play an overwhelmingly dominant role."

GiveDirectly has spent months identifying the biggest barriers to rapidly growing its antipoverty work, according to Nick Allardice, its president and CEO. The tech-focused nonprofit sends cash straight to poor households with no strings attached.

Recipients must have mobile phones to receive the digital transfers. GiveDirectly offers phones for about US$15, usually subtracted from recipients' first payment. So the nonprofit secured investments this year to build out a supply chain to support many more mobile phones going forward.

The group is betting that its preparations for a charitable boom will be worthwhile.

"I have this level of cautious optimism," Allardice said. "But I can't foresee the future, and I don't know exactly what's going to happen."

Wild Animal Initiative executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb shares those tempered expectations.

His nonprofit funds wild animal welfare research. It's the sort of work some observers predict will see the biggest upswings in support: nonprofits connected to effective altruism, a data-driven movement that prioritises donations to causes with the greatest impact on the most living beings.

The movement's reputation took a hit when Sam Bankman-Fried, one of its leading proponents and financial backers, got a 25-year prison sentence for cryptocurrency fraud. But the ideas are rebounding in the same tech circles that could see big payouts as more AI companies go public.

Effective altruists have learned not to rely too heavily on any one funder, according to Shorb. He expects "quite a bit" of fresh support for animal advocacy and sees an outsize role for midsize donors.

He said he has connected with a couple of Anthropic employees. Perhaps more important, he said, are relationships with the philanthropic advisers who help plan donors' giving.

"As you can imagine, it's a pretty tricky place for a soon-to-be billionaire to be to have all this potential power coming soon," Shorb said. "As soon as anyone finds out about that, anyone who can possibly get their email or phone number will just be knocking down their door. So we've tried to be gentle and slow and respectful in our approach."

data.title: Oil prices fall amid equity selloff though Iran war attacks limit losses
data.description:
PERTH — Oil prices fell on Monday (Nov 23) as the selloff in the wider financial markets amid concerns about the ability of the AI sector to boost economic growth spilled over into commodities, though the continuing attacks on Gulf shipping limited the losses.

Crude dropped, adding to its three-week losing streak, amid the overall negative sentiment in global financial markets as Asian equities opened lower on Monday, with the tech-heavy South Korean market down four per cent and China, Hong Kong and Australia all falling. US equity markets have also slumped with the Nasdaq plunging 10 per cent last week.

Brent crude futures fell 28 cents, or 0.30 per cent, to US$92.29 (S$120) a barrel by 2.16am GMT (10.16am SGT). US West Texas Intermediate futures fell 15 cents, or 0.18 per cent, to us$83.26 a barrel.

Brent declined four per cent last week and WTI five per cent.

Still, the fighting from the unresolved US-Israeli war against Iran continues to limit any losses. On Sunday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery and over the weekend multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz were reported.

"It's momentum carrying (oil) down," said Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at Sydney-based XAnalysts. But he cautioned that the shipping attacks are having an effect as "ballast (empty) vessels counts are building in crude while laden vessels are not. This risk to flows will start to price soon".

In Turkey, talks on Sunday at the global climate summit COP31 collapsed for the first time since 2009 after nations could not come to an agreement over including a statement on the phase-out of fossil fuels in a final text.

Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing countries have said fossil fuels will play a role in the economy for the foreseeable future and they lobbied to keep any mention of fossil fuels out of the text, observers at the summit said.

OPEC had earlier defended fossil fuel use at the summit.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia.

data.title: CPF Board, Singtel complete transfer of special discounted shares to CDP accounts
data.description:
Holders of Singtel's Special Discounted Shares (SDS) can now hold and manage their shares directly, following the completion of transfer from CPF Board to the Central Depository (CDP) on Nov 21.

In an joint news release on Monday (Nov 23), Singtel Group and CPF Board said that about 406,000 of the 615,000 SDS holders have transferred 477 million SDS to their CDP accounts.

Meanwhile, about 209,000, or 34 per cent, sold their shares.

"Leading up to the transfer, CPF Board and Singtel worked closely to reach out to SDS holders through individual notifications as well as various publicity and outreach efforts, including in-person and online touchpoints," they added.

CPF Board and Singtel reiterated that no action is needed for those who wish to continue holding their Singtel SDS, noting that designated CDP accounts have been created for about one-third of the 406,000, who were without an account.

Those holding individual CDP accounts will now have their Singtel SDS consolidated with other securities in their CDP accounts and any other Singtel ordinary shares they may be holding.

If they wish to sell their Singtel SDS, they can do so via an SGX-registered brokerage that they have a trading account with. 

As for SDS holders with designated CDP accounts created in their name, they can sell their shares through Philip Securities website, in person at SingPost, or select SGX retail brokers.

Notification and scam advisory

All SDS holders will receive a hardcopy notification letter from CPF Board, CDP and Singtel by mid-December, informing them of the transfer completion.

CPF Board also advised its members to remain vigilant against scams, noting that some scammers may fabricate stories about members' Singtel SDS to deceive them.

The board advised those who received messages, email, or QR code which allegedly directs them to the SDS website to first verify the URL's authenticity. The official website is https://sds.singtel.com. 

Singtel's group chief financial officer Arthur Lang said the transfer of SDs shares to CDP accounts was ultimately about giving holders a choice and enabling them to exercise their rights as shareholders directly.

"As we move forward, our focus remains on executing our strategy, investing for sustainable growth and creating long-term value for all our shareholders," he added.

data.title: Annual Value thresholds for social support schemes to be raised from March 2027
data.description:
The Government will raise the Annual Value (AV) thresholds used to determine eligibility for social support schemes from March 1, 2027, announced the Ministry of Finance (MOF) on Monday (Nov 23).

The move intends to ensure that Singaporeans living in HDB flats and lower-value private properties will continue to qualify for a range of support schemes as the AV of many residential properties increased since 2025, when the AVs were last adjusted, said MOF.

By adjusting the thresholds, the Government aims to ensure that Singaporeans with greater needs do not lose access to support schemes solely because of higher property valuations.

The AV of a home, alongside other criteria such as income, is one of several indicators used to assess eligibility and determine the level of benefits an individual or household may receive under schemes including the GST Voucher scheme, MediShield Life premium subsidies and the Workfare Income Supplement scheme.

Those living in properties with lower AVs generally receive higher levels of support.

Currently, households fall into two AV tiers: Homes with an AV of up to $21,000, and homes with an AV of more than $21,000 but not exceeding $31,000. 

From March 1, 2027, the thresholds will be revised upwards. 

The first AV tier will increase to up to $24,000, while the second AV tier will rise to more than $24,000 and up to $32,000.

Eligibility for social support schemes in a given year is based on the preceding year's AV. 

This means that eligibility for 2027 benefits will be assessed using a household's or individual's 2026 AV.

The Government said it will continue reviewing its social support schemes and eligibility criteria to ensure support remains targeted at Singaporeans with greater needs.

Singaporeans seeking more information can approach the respective government agencies administering the various schemes.

data.title: One-off property tax rebate for all owner-occupied residential properties in 2027
data.description:
Homeowners in Singapore will receive a one-off property tax rebate in 2027, with HDB flat owners getting a 15 per cent reduction and private residential property owners receiving a 10 per cent rebate capped at $100.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) and The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (Iras) announced the rebates on Monday (Nov 23), saying the move aims to cushion property tax payments amid cost-of-living concerns.

The rebates will be automatically offset against the property tax payable in homeowners' 2027 tax bills.

After the rebates, owner-occupiers living in three-room and larger HDB flats can expect to pay an average of about $2 to $4 more in property tax per month.

Most owner-occupiers of private residential properties will see an average increase of about $6 per month.

Those living in one-room and two-room HDB flats will continue to pay no property tax.

HDB flat values updated to reflect market rents

As part of its annual review, the Government has updated the Annual Values (AVs) of HDB flats to better reflect prevailing market rents in their respective towns.

Property tax bills are due by Jan 31, 2027.

All property owners will receive their 2027 property tax bills by December 2026.

Iras will notify property owners via SMS and/or email when their bills are available for viewing on the myTax Portal.

As the tax bills will be issued in batches, some homeowners may receive theirs earlier than others.

The payment deadline is Jan 31, 2027.

Property owners are encouraged to pay through GIRO, either in interest-free monthly instalments of up to 12 months or through a one-time deduction.

Eligible retiree owner-occupiers aged 65 and above, with an assessable income of $39,000 or below, may apply for an extended GIRO instalment plan of up to 24 months to make their payments.

data.title: He gave up an iron rice bowl and sold his home to chase his business dreams
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Kelvin Hong spent seven years in the civil service before giving up the security of public service to pursue his entrepreneurial dream – establishing a vocational school and a chain of spa and wellness outlets.

As a civil servant, he worked on economic policy, including writing the first policy paper setting out the Government’s approach to fighting SARS, or severe acute respiratory syndrome.

Having previously enjoyed the security of an “iron rice bowl” career, he now had to make difficult financial decisions to fund his business.

He sold his condominium unit and moved his family of five to a rental property, and later downsized to an HDB resale flat, all while dealing with the uncertainty of running a business and providing for his family.

He sold his chain of wellness outlets in 2010.

“Education has always been a passion of mine. I’ve been tutoring since my university days and have accumulated about 28 years of experience teaching economics,” said Hong, 52, who founded The Economics Tutor in 1998 while running other businesses.

Throughout his entrepreneurial journey, he continued to tutor in economics, a passion he had developed at university.

After selling his other businesses, he decided to focus fully on tuition.

Today, Hong is the founder and principal tutor of The Economics Tutor and Ace GP Tuition, where he helps pre-university students build a strong foundation in economics and General Paper.

He graduated from the National University of Singapore with a Bachelor of Social Sciences, with first-class honours in economics.

His wife, 50, is also his partner in the tuition business, and they have three children aged 22, 20 and 11.

Do you invest in anything? If yes, what do you invest in and why?

The Economics Tutor and Ace GP Tuition are my current ventures. I have run and sold off other businesses over the last two decades.

I prefer investing in my businesses because making money on its own has never given me much joy. What I enjoy is creating something and developing it until it succeeds, because by then, it adds real value to society. I am also considering other business ventures in the tech and education space.

I don’t own any individual stocks at the moment. My savings sit in safe assets. They won’t make anyone rich, but they’re secure. I’ve been tempted to buy a few individual stocks over the past year, but prices have looked too high to me, so I’m keeping dry powder and waiting for a correction rather than chasing the market. Knowing when not to invest is part of investing too.

My children’s education isn’t a financial asset in the usual sense, but it’s the investment I’m most certain of. Besides carefully choosing tuition that deepens their understanding and mastery beyond exams, I invest heavily in building their competencies: carpentry, baking, art and craft, music, robotics, various sports and communication skills, as well as their own little start-ups.

What’s your biggest or most valuable asset right now?

On paper, probably my home. But the asset that actually pays the bills is my tuition business. Unlike most assets, it doesn’t depreciate as long as I keep using it.

What’s your approach when it comes to growing your money?

Spend less than you earn, don’t borrow what you can’t comfortably repay, don’t buy what you don’t understand, work really hard, and be patient.

None of it is original, but after working on economic policy and then running businesses through good years and bad, I’ve found that most financial disasters come from impatience: wanting the return without putting in the time or effort.

A lot of what passes for investment advice online today is really marketing. If someone is promising high returns with no risk, the question I’d ask is – who is actually making money from the arrangement?

Do you invest in any tangible assets?

No. As an economist, I find it hard to love an asset that pays no income and whose value depends entirely on another person fancying it. The closest I came to tangible assets was a small property portfolio, which I have since sold.

What was your first exposure to investing, and what was your first investment?

My first real investment, in the sense of putting serious money at risk, was buying some stocks on the Singapore Exchange and some unit trusts. I don’t think they fared well. I was a greenhorn who had just started earning serious money and was happily experimenting. In hindsight, there are cheaper ways to learn.

What has been your biggest financial mistake?

In a previous business, an overseas outlet ended in a six-figure loss. Looking back, I had made the classic mistake of planning around the demand I hoped for rather than the demand I could actually see. I now use that outlet as a case study when I teach company strategies. Students remember a real six-figure mistake far better than a textbook example.

What has been your best financial decision?

My best financial decision was to sell off, in 2010, my chain of wellness outlets. It was a multimillion-dollar business, but my greatest returns came in the form of a sabbatical to reset my spiritual condition, including my lifestyle and life goals.

I traded in my business world back then for my soul, and it has been my best investment to date. During those sabbatical years, I was still providing tuition, albeit on a very small scale, and I have built it up since then into my current ventures.

Money-wise, what were your growing-up years like?

My mum was a homemaker and my dad was a senior executive in a multinational corporation. It was a comfortable childhood, and maybe that is why I was rather spendthrift as a young adult.

I did start working early, selling Newsweek subscriptions and tutoring during my varsity days, so I was earning my own money from about 18. That taught me what an hour of my time was worth, and that the most reliable way to earn more was to become better at something people needed.

What was your first job?

Selling Newsweek subscriptions in schools during the holidays was my first lesson in selling – a few minutes in front of strangers to make my case and far more noes than yeses.

I learnt that selling is mostly about informing people in a persuasive way, which turns out not to be so different from teaching. I don’t remember exactly what it paid, but it was decent money for someone my age.

As a child, what did you save up for?

I don’t recall actually saving up for anything. I was more of a spender as a child. I learnt to save only as I became wiser and more mature.

My students sometimes assume I live a lavish, branded lifestyle, and I tell them it’s quite the opposite: When I need to shop, I mostly do it online or in Johor Bahru.

When did you first realise money is important?

Honestly, not until I was near 30, when two big responsibilities arrived almost at once. I had left the civil service to start my business, and suddenly, I had staff whose salaries had to be paid every month. Around the same time, my wife and I started our family.

Before that, money was something I earned and spent on myself. After that, other people’s livelihoods were in my hands, and so was my own young family’s. Money stopped being about what I could buy, and became about the people I was responsible for.

Where is home for you?

I live in a semi-detached house in the east.

What car do you drive?

I don’t own a car and I don’t drive. I take public transport, which, in Singapore, is excellent.

What would your perfect day look like?

A swim or pickleball game followed by brunch with my wife and, ideally, at least one of my children. Then class prep and lessons from early afternoon all the way till 10pm, ending with a late dinner while my children have some desserts.

What would you do if you suddenly had a windfall of $1 million?

Very little would change as it won’t be enough to buy me a school. But I’d set aside more for my children’s university costs, keep the rest in safe assets like T-bills, and wait patiently for the right opportunity.

If you suddenly had only $100 to your name, what would you do?

I’d boost my social media accounts to market my businesses. If I lost everything else, I’d still have the ability to teach, and that has never needed much capital to get going.

I would also write a book titled Riches To Rags to share valuable lessons and hopefully turn it into a bestseller and a popular podcast.

This article was first published in The Straits Times. Permission required for reproduction.

data.title: Chinese electric car brand JMEV shuts down Singapore showroom a year after opening
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Chinese electric vehicle (EV) brand JMEV came to Singapore in July 2025 but its showroom in the east has closed after just a year or so.

The brand’s distributor Valor Auto was incorporated on July 2, 2024, launching the brand a year later. JMEV was one of 15 or so Chinese EV brands that have entered Singapore since 2024.

It is the second brand to exit Singapore in recent months. Chinese car brand Neta – made by Shanghai-based Hozon Auto – closed shop in early April 2025, less than three months after opening day.

The JMEV showroom, housed in a mixed development in Telok Kurau Road, was empty, and most of the windows were boarded up when The Straits Times visited on Nov 18.

Its Singapore website was not accessible, and a call to the official phone number on Nov 19 was answered by someone who said she did not have ties to the dealership. The brand’s marketing manager, when contacted, said she was no longer with the company, but did not give further details.

Some 28 units of the JMEV Elight four-door electric saloon have been registered since 2025, with the most recent one registered in June 2026, according to Land Transport Authority records.

Based on the last publicly available price list dated in May, the cars are sold with a 10-year battery warranty, five-year vehicle warranty and six years of routine servicing. The model was priced at $208,777 with a certificate of entitlement before applicable discounts.

Mahaendra Gofar, a veteran of the automotive sector who has worked for car firms in Germany and China, said it is common practice for distributors to offer extended warranty coverage that goes beyond what the manufacturer offers.

If the dealership folds, the local portion of the warranty will no longer be valid. The terms of the factory warranty are not stated in the price list.

Lawyer Parwani Vijai said affected owners have no legal recourse if the distributor closes.

In response to The Straits Times, Melvin Yong, president of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE), said it did not receive any complaints against the distributor between Jan 1 and Nov 18.

“CASE advises consumers to conduct due diligence before committing to a vehicle purchase.

“This includes checking the distributor’s track record, reputation, financial standing, the long-term availability of warranty and after-sales support, and other alternatives should the distributorship close,” he said, adding that consumers who are affected may approach CASE for help.

Experts said owners are not completely without options in terms of service support if a brand exits the market.

When it comes to parts, Ler Hwee Tiong, director of an after-market workshop chain, said the supply chain in automobile production is robust in China.

So even if a carmaker is out of business, owners should be able to source most parts directly through popular shopping portals like Aliexpress.

In JMEV’s case, its parent company Jiangling Motors Corporation Group is operational in China and active in export markets including Chile, Morocco and Myanmar.

Basic mechanical work, Gofar said, should be manageable for independent motor workshops, but owners may be stranded when it comes to proprietary software updates.

Describing the Chinese automotive industry to be in a state of flux, the experts expect consolidations down the road, where carmakers may merge or exit altogether.

Gofar said consumers need to find out more about how the brands are doing in their home country as well as the background of their appointed distributors in Singapore before committing to a purchase, while Ler said larger and more established brands are “safer bets”.

The influx of new Chinese car brands is not unique to Singapore, and Gofar said rules are needed to better protect consumer interests after the car is bought.

For instance, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Commerce fined and suspended a dealer in August for failing to provide spare parts, going as far as summoning the manufacturer to ensure that consumers are supported, he added.

This article was first published in The Straits Times. Permission required for reproduction.

data.title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%
data.description:
NEW YORK - President Donald Trump said Saturday (Nov 21) that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfil a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.

"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's Saturday in America.

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10 per cent. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2 per cent, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.

Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.

The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfil Trump's promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."

Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.

"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley posted on X on Saturday.

Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly US$100 billion (S$130 billion) in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10 per cent. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.

About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed US$160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.

Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about US$1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

2. Hold up. What do interest rate, EIR and processing fees mean?

There's quite a bit of jargon here, so let's go through some points of confusion that may be swimming around in your head.

Interest rates

Notice that interest rates are quoted as “from X%” instead of being stated simply as “X%”? That’s because personal loans are pretty dynamic as they all depend on factors such as your credit history and the loan amount.

EIR

EIR stands for Effective Interest Rate. Taking into consideration other fees (like processing fee; see next point) and the loan repayment schedule, it is a more accurate reflection of the cost of borrowing than the advertised interest rates.

Processing fees

This is the main hidden cost of personal loans and is worth highlighting. The processing fee is deducted from the principal—meaning, for a $10,000 loan with a $100 (or 1%) processing fee, you get only $9,900 in cash. As a borrower, you might not “feel” it, but it does eat into your funds and increase the cost of borrowing.

Now, let's walk through the 10 featured personal loan packages.

3. DBS Personal Loan

The DBS personal loan is only open to existing customers. If you already have (1) a DBS Cashline account or have a DBS credit card and (2) credit your salary into a DBS deposit account, you can get the cash disbursed instantly.

The loan is open to Singaporeans and PRs, as well as foreigners with DBS Cashline or credit card accounts. You must be aged 21 to 70 years with a minimum annual income of $20,000-this opens up DBS personal loans to include slightly older groups of people and lower income earners compared to other banks.

Like the Standard Chartered CashOne loan, you don't need to earn a regular salary to be eligible for this loan. Self-employed individuals and commission earners can also apply.

DBS's personal loan promises interest rates as low as 1.48 per cent. There is a processing fee of 1 per cent, bringing the lowest possible EIR to 3.22 per cent. Loan tenures of 6 months to 5 years are available.

Do note that these are the lowest possible rates and the actual interest rate depends on what DBS is prepared to extend to you.

4. Trust Instant Loan

When they say "instant", they mean it. Trust's personal loan, called Trust Instant Loan, disburses cash to you in just 60 seconds with the Trust credit card.

This is how it works: You have a Trust credit card with a certain available credit balance at any one point in time. The Trust Instant Loan converts a portion of that balance into cash for you. Spend that cash on anything you want!

The Trust Instant Loan is open to all Trust customers. Given how it works, as I just explained above, you do need to have a Trust credit card to be eligible. But this isn't a bad thing-for one thing, it makes repaying the loan seamless. Each month, you'll see your loan instalment charged to your credit card bill. To pay the instalment, simply pay through your credit card statement via your Trust App.

The Trust Instant Loan is also EXTRA affordable with an interest rate starting from just 1.00 per cent p.a. (EIR from 2.28 per cent p.a.). They also charge no processing fees, annual fees, or the like. However, there is a three per cent early repayment fee on your remaining loan amount if you repay the rest of your loan early.

The Trust Instant Loan is open to Singapore Citizens, PRs, and Foreigners aged 21 to 65 years old. You could be a salaried worker, commission-based, or self-employed as long as your annual income is $30,000 for Singaporeans or $60,000 for Foreigners.

5. CIMB Personal Loan

The CIMB Personal Loan is another personal loan that comes with no processing fees. Its interest rate currently starts from 0.89 per cent p.a. (EIR from 1.72 per cent p.a.). This is because of an ongoing 11.11 promotion (till Nov 18). You're essentially getting a 0.11 per cent interest rebate when you apply for a loan in this period. Make sure it has a tenure of between 12 to 60 months.

You also get flexible loan tenure options of 12, 24, 36, 48 or 60 months.

For shorter loan tenures of three or six months, you could also get 0 per cent interest. But that does come with a one-time processing fee of 0.99 per cent (EIR of 5.99 per cent p.a.).

As far as eligibility goes, the CIMB Personal Loan is fairly standard. It's open to Singapore Citizens and Singapore PRs with a minimum annual income of $20,000, and to Malaysians earning at least $30,000 a year.

You'll also need to be 21 to 70 years old-that maximum age sits between the Citibank and DBS personal loan age limit. There's no prerequisite to have a CIMB Bank Account or CIMB credit card before you apply, so go ahead as long as you meet the criteria above.

Like any personal loan, you'll incur a penalty fee if you try to repay it early. For the CIMB Personal Loan, this fee is three per cent of the outstanding loan amount or $250, whichever is higher.

6. UOB Personal Loan

UOB's personal loan is only open to existing UOB credit cardholders or CashPlus customers who are Singaporeans, PRs aged 21 to 65. You'll also need to be a salaried worker earning at least $30,000 a year. Not an existing UOB customer? You'll have to get a UOB credit card or CashPlus to apply for a UOB Personal Loan.

The interest rate is from 1.00 per cent p.a. for loan periods of 12, 24, 36, 48 or 60 months, with a 1.93 per cent p.a. EIR.

While UOB used to only waive processing fees for loan periods 24 months and up, processing fees are now waived for all loan periods.

If you're an existing UOB customer, you can get instant approval when you apply for your personal loan online.

7. Standard Chartered CashOne

Standard Chartered CashOne personal loan is open to Singapore Citizens, PRs and foreigners with a Singapore Employment Pass aged 21 and above.

The barriers to entry for the Standard Chartered CashOne personal loan have gone up slightly. The minimum annual income requirements are now $30,000 for Singaporeans and PRs and $90,000 for foreigners. You also don't necessarily need to be a salaried worker to apply-Standard Chartered is cool with salaried employees, variable/commission-based employees, and even self-employed individuals.

You can apply for this personal loan online by signing in through Singpass and receive your loan disbursement within 15 minutes-it's super easy. There's no need to be an existing Standard Chartered customer to get this personal loan.

So, it's fast-but is it also affordable? Standard Chartered charges an initial annual fee of $199 (deducted from your approved loan) for any loan tenure between one to five years. From the second year onwards, you won't have to pay any more annual fees — unless you miss any instalments, in which case you will pay $50 in annual fees for that year. 

Plus the late payment fee of $100. If you pay your full monthly instalment on time for the first six months, you won't have to worry about late penalties. After that, you'll have the flexibility to pay just the minimum-whichever is lower: $50 or one per cent of your approved monthly principal.

So taking the $199 annual fee into consideration, I'd say CashOne is more worthwhile if you're taking out a big loan.

Interest rates are advertised as starting from 0.90 per cent, working out to an EIR of 1.75 per cent and above. In reality, interest rates are personalised, so yours might differ from this example.

8. HSBC Personal Loan

HSBC's personal loan is open to Singaporeans and PRs aged 21 to 65 years old with an annual income of $30,000 and above for salaried workers, and $40,000 for self-employed or commission-based workers. Foreigners must earn at least $60,000 a year and have an employment pass with at least six months' validity.

The best part about HSBC's personal loan is its long loan tenure of up to seven years — currently the longest loan tenure in Singapore. So if you need to borrow a large sum but can't afford high monthly repayments, HSBC's personal loan is definitely one you should consider.

HSBC has dropped their promotional interest rates even further now starting from 1.30 per cent p.a. with an EIR from 2.50 per cent p.a. with no processing fees. Remember, however, that actual interest rates will vary from person to person.

Another factor to consider is that HSBC's personal loan comes with an annual fee of $120, and only the first year's fee is waived. Don't miss your payments, or you'll be subject to a $120 late payment fee.

9. GXS FlexiLoan

GXS is a digital bank that's 60 per cent owned by Grab and 40 per cent owned by Singtel. Now, don't be dissuaded by the idea of a digital bank. Like any regular bank, GXS offers customers a personal loan-and a decent one at that.

With a loan tenure between two and 60 months, GXS FlexiLoan instalment plan interest rates could start from as low as 1.00 per cent p.a.. However, do note that you'll only receive this advertised rate if you name your loan "MSDEAL". Another caveat here is that this lower rate will be awarded as cashback. Meaning to say actual advertised rates hover at around 2.88 per cent p.a. (EIR from 5.45 per cent p.a.).

On top of all that, GXS FlexiLoan doesn't charge any annual, processing, early repayment or late fees-something almost unheard of when it comes to loans from your traditional banks. You heard that right, repay your loan early with no extra charges! However, GXS will charge you late interest if your repayments are late, so you won't get off scot-free.

One downside to the GXS FlexiLoan is that foreigners aren't eligible. It's only for Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents between 21 and 65 years old. The minimum annual income is $20,000.

10. MariBank Instant Loan

The MariBank Instant Loan is a fully digital personal loan that focuses on speed and simplicity. It offers a starting interest rate of 1.28 per cent p.a. with an EIR from 1.92 per cent p.a., and there are no processing fees, which helps keep borrowing costs down.

You can choose loan tenures ranging from three to 60 months, and once approved, funds are typically disbursed almost instantly. While the loan is tied to a Mari Credit Card, you don't need to be an existing cardholder-one will be issued automatically upon approval.

Eligibility is limited to Singapore Citizens and PRs aged 21 and above with a minimum annual income of S$30,000. Applications are done entirely via the MariBank app, using Singpass.

Do note that early repayment incurs a fee of three per cent of the outstanding amount or S$100 (whichever is higher), and missed payments may attract high credit card interest charges, so this loan is best for borrowers who can commit to regular repayments.

11. Citibank Quick Cash with Ready Credit (New Customers)

I'm going to preface this by saying that the 3.45 per cent (EIR from 6.50 per cent) interest rate for the Citi Quick Cash personal loan is only available to customers who are completely new to Citibank loans. If you already have a Citibank loan, you'll be given a higher interest rate.

The plus point for this one is definitely the ease of getting your funds. You'll be easily able to convert the credit balance on your Citi Credit Card or Citibank Ready Credit account into cash. Just log into the Citi Mobile App, key in the amount of cash you need and you can get the funds pretty much instantly.

Citi Quick Cash is open to Singapore Citizens and PRs (salaried or self-employed) with a minimum annual income of $30,000, and foreigners with an annual income of at least $42,000. The eligible age range is 21 to 65 years.

With Citibank's Quick Cash personal loan, you can choose a tenure of 12, 24, 36, 48, or 60 months-all with zero processing fees. You'll get a 3.56 per cent interest rate on Citibank's personal loan with a shorter 1-year tenure, or 3.45 per cent if you intend to extend your loan repayment to three years. While the interest rates differ according to tenure period, you'll get an EIR of 6.5 per cent for all.

That said, don't take our word for it. Rates are customised, so its best to enquire with the bank directly.

12. OCBC ExtraCash Personal Loan

While the OCBC ExtraCash Personal Loan has the highest interest rates (from 5.43 per cent p.a. / EIR from 11.47 per cent p.a.) on this list, it does come with some perks that might make it a solid choice for some. If you need a large loan, you can borrow up to six times your monthly income, with fixed repayments spread over 12 to 60 months.

Like many of the other loans mentioned, it offers fast disbursement when you sign up via Myinfo. Plus, it has a relatively low entry requirement — just $20,000 in annual income for Singaporeans and PRs. You'll also be able to easily see a full breakdown of all your outstanding payments via internet banking.

However, punctual repayments are a must. A late payment will set you back $80, and if you decide to restructure or repay early, you'll be charged a three per cent fee on your outstanding balance. So, be sure of your loan tenure before committing!

Whatever personal loan package you choose, opt for the smallest loan amount and shortest term you can comfortably manage. This will keep your interest payments to a minimum.

Remember that the actual interest rate a bank offers you will depend on factors like your credit history, how much you want to borrow and for how long. So if you don't get offered the lowest advertised interest rates with one bank, it's worth comparing what other banks can offer to find the cheapest personal loan for your profile.

There are certain groups of individuals that may have a harder time taking out a personal loan.

Older individuals: If you're above 65 years old, DBS/POSB and CIMB will let you apply for personal loans up to the age of 70 years.

Those earning an annual income below $30,000: Most of the loans I've listed above have a minimum requirement of about $20,000 annual income, so you have plenty of options if this pertains to you.

Commission-based workers or self-employed individuals: Citibank Quick Cash, HSBC Personal Loan, DBS Personal Loan and Standard Chartered CashOne are good options. Some other banks may only accept salaried workers.

14. Term loan vs credit line-which should you choose?

While researching personal loans, you might have come across many different loan types, some of which do not seem to fit what we described above.

We usually recommend these loans because they have much lower interest rates. You can pay back slowly and steadily at a pace comfortable to your financial situation.

Many banks also offer a personal line of credit-sometimes called a credit line, revolving loan, or even "flexible repayment loan".

This is a pre-approved amount of money you can cash out in part or whole, but you need to repay it ASAP or else face sky-high interest rates. Don't fall for it unless you're absolutely confident you can pay the money back immediately.

These days, most banks base their personal loans on either your personal line of credit or credit card limit. So you will need either a credit card or credit line to get the loan. However, it is still considered a term loan if it comes with a structured repayment plan.

But before you sign up, understand that your credit cards with this bank will be as good as dead because you'll have effectively "spent" your credit on a cash loan.

15. Being in debt is not fun…

But it can be prevented. If you must take out a loan, channel all your energies into paying it off on time to avoid late charges. In the meantime, re-examine your income and budget, making a note of everything you spend on, so you won't have to resort to loans again.

Ideally, you should draw up a budget that gives you enough leeway to set aside some cash for the future without starving to death.

You should also build up an emergency fund worth a few months' expenses. If you're hit with unforeseen circumstances, you can dip into this fund instead of having to take a loan.

It's also a good idea to know what types of insurance you need. We recommend hospitalisation insurance at a bare minimum, and life insurance if you have dependents. Being sufficiently insured ensures that you don't get hit with huge bills if the unexpected happens.
